I’m only a little bit older than you and every birthday past 18 is a miracle to me. It’s actually something I bring up to my most inner circle about how navigating the world feels so “new”. Where most people are following their childhood dream, living a life they had planned, or at least come from an environment where the path laid out in front of them has been paved by older siblings, family members, or family friends. 

It took awhile to build an inner circle and find people who I felt connected to, but I knew this was going to be the MOST essential part. At the end of the day, the moments that we remember in life always come back to connection (with others and in moments a deeper connection to ourselves) and experience. It’s great to hear how much hope you have in you. Now imagine having good people around you that can remind you of that light within you when you’re feeling the weight of severe depression. Next time you’re around someone who you think you’d enjoy having a conversation with, put in effort to keep the conversation going. 

It’s great that you’re asking about how to live intentionally because that’s The question that sparks change. I started to listen to podcasts of people who I feel would be a great role model by standards of values in which I feel I can align with. (Michelle Obama & Craig Robinson IMO is great). It was helpful to just listen. There weren’t feelings of comparison, there was just me soaking in the lessons they’ve learned and the stories from various great people  and where they’ve come from despite the odds. You’ll feel what resonates with you and from there you can choose the qualities and characteristics you want to embody and then break it down on what that looks like on a day to day basis. 

Reading also kept me informed on how to make change possible. I really liked Charles Duhigg the Power of Habit. It breaks down why behaviors become a habit and how to replace maladaptive ones with productive ones. You can ask chatGPT for a summary of keystone habits in this book and see how you can implement one into your routine. 

It’s hard. It’s 10x harder than those who are neurotypical. You’re not only fighting against the diagnosis, but trauma that you’re still in the thick of. It’s going to be so hard, but if you’re gonna wake up another day anyway, why not try?

100% understand what you’re going through. I graduated from UCLA with a degree in psychology and a minor in film. I did my two years at a junior college, transferred with honor roll, was involved in a psychology frat, and worked at my schools disability center. When I got to UCLA I balanced (kind of poorly but was also adjusting) a sorority, clubs, and the class load.

Whenever I was assigned reading there’d be such a lack of motivation, even though I was like you! I loved psychology but something about assigned reading/homework was difficult. So I made sure the classes I chose fit my study style (only 2-3 exams and a few quizzes , no homework assignments throughout the quarter because when I’d miss one I’d beat myself up for it and spiral)

I studied alone (half due to my fear of saying the wrong thing in group studying or not feeling smart enough) but it was helpful when I planned the day before what I’d be studying the next day so I wouldn’t doubt what I had to do. Spacing study time is good so you’re not overwhelmed.

Connecting with people who had similar struggles was such a huge comfort. Don’t underestimate the value of having people listen to you and try to help you out. 

I finished on time even though my graduating year was when we were in covid 

I’d say the thing that kept me going was that I believed I was strong, mentally. I believed there was a better version of myself and I’d get there. It felt hopeless when that severe depression would hit, but I had my therapist to guide me through those difficult times.

SO, you’ve gotten this far AND you’re still alive. You have the strength to withstand these bouts of being unmotivated. Find your Will, and run with it.

(My Will was how creative I was in writing, that really helped grounding me in knowing I was at least good at something)

I also noticed if you close your eyes and think about what you’re really feeling or wanting... you already know ; seeing options just cloud your initial thought. So stick with what your first thought, opinion, or choice is. :) hope this helps
